subject: math
title: Geometry II: Volume, Surface Area, and Scale
objectives: You will tell volume from surface area and read the GED formula sheet, knowing what B, p, h, s, and r stand for.
You will find the volume and surface area of rectangular prisms, other prisms, and cylinders.
You will find the volume and surface area of pyramids and cones, choosing height or slant height and using the Pythagorean theorem when one is missing.
You will find the volume and surface area of spheres, combine solids into composite figures, and work backward from a volume to a missing dimension.
You will use scale drawings and scale factors to find actual lengths, areas, and volumes.

slides.title: Week 6 Math: Geometry II
slides.board:
Volume, Surface Area, and Scale

  • Tell volume from surface area; read the formula sheet (B, p, h, s, r)
  • Prisms and cylinders
  • Pyramids and cones: height or slant height?
  • Spheres, composite solids, and working backward
  • Scale drawings and scale factors

Today: warm-up, five solids, composite shapes, scale, two GED-style questions, strategy

notes.say: Last week you measured flat shapes. This week we stand them up and make them solid: boxes, cans, cones, balls, and the scale drawings used to plan them. Here is the best news of the week: you do not have to memorize a single formula, because the GED hands you a formula sheet. What the test checks is whether you can read that sheet and put the right number in the right letter. As always, I explain, I show you an example, we do some together, and then you try some on your own.
ask: Have you ever had to figure out how much something holds, like a tank or a pool, or how much paint or paper covers something? (expected answer: any; use their example later in the lesson)
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 5 min (slide 2); volume vs. surface area and the formula sheet 6 min (slides 3–4); prisms and cylinders 12 min (slides 5–9); pyramids and cones 11 min (slides 10–14); spheres, composite solids, and working backward 10 min (slides 15–20); scale 11 min (slides 21–26); strategy and recap 5 min (slides 27–28). If you fall behind, cut the we-do slides to two problems each. Have the student open a copy of the formula sheet now.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 5 Review
slides.board:
Use 3.14 for π. Calculator allowed.

  1. Area of a rectangle 9 ft by 6 ft
  2. Area of a triangle with base 10 in and height 7 in
  3. Area of a circle with radius 5 cm
  4. Circumference of a circle with diameter 8 m
  5. A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. How long is the hypotenuse?

notes.say: These are last week's skills, and every one of them comes back today. Problems 1, 2, and 3 are areas of flat shapes, and today those become the base of a solid, the letter B on the formula sheet. Problem 4 is a distance around, which is what the letter p means. Problem 5 is the Pythagorean theorem, which we will use to find a slant height. Take three minutes, then read me your answers.
ask: In problem 3, what did you square, and why? (expected answer: the radius, 5, because the area formula is πr<sup>2</sup>)
In problem 4, did you use the radius or the diameter? (expected answer: the diameter, because C = πd)
notes.watch: On problem 2, 70 means the ½ was forgotten. On problem 3, 31.4 means the student multiplied 3.14 × 5 × 2 (doubling instead of squaring); write 5<sup>2</sup> = 5 × 5 on the board. On problem 4, 12.56 means they halved the diameter and used C = πd anyway. On problem 5, 14 means they added the legs. Each of these errors returns today, so note which ones you see.

slides.title: Volume or Surface Area?
slides.board:
VolumeSurface area
Question it answersHow much does it hold?How much material covers it?
What you measureThe space insideThe total area of every outside face
UnitsCubic: in3, ft3, m3Square: in2, ft2, m2
Key wordsfill, hold, capacity, pourpaint, wrap, cover, label

A box 3 by 2 by 2 holds 12 unit cubes: V = 12 cubic units.

notes.say: Every solid has two different measurements, and the GED will tell you which one it wants through its wording. Volume counts how many little unit cubes fit inside, so its units are cubed. Surface area adds up the flat areas of every outside face, like unfolding the box flat and measuring the cardboard, so its units are squared. Before you touch a formula, decide: is this question about filling or about covering?
ask: Water in a fish tank: volume or surface area? (expected answer: volume)
The label wrapped around a soup can: volume or surface area? (expected answer: surface area)
Why is volume in cubic units? (expected answer: it counts cubes; length × width × height multiplies three lengths)
notes.watch: Some students think a "full" object always means volume. Ask about a basketball: the air inside is volume, but the leather on it is surface area. The object does not decide; the question does.

slides.title: Reading the Formula Sheet
slides.board:
SolidVolumeSurface area
PrismV = BhSA = ph + 2B
CylinderV = πr2hSA = 2πrh + 2πr2
PyramidV = (1/3)BhSA = ½ps + B
ConeV = (1/3)πr2hSA = πrs + πr2
SphereV = (4/3)πr3SA = 4πr2

B = area of the base   p = perimeter of the base   h = height (straight up)   s = slant height (down the side)   r = radius

notes.say: This table is on the GED formula sheet, so your job is to read it, not memorize it. Notice the patterns. A capital B is always an area, and a small p is always a length around the base, so do not mix them up. Prisms and cylinders have two bases, so their surface area ends in plus 2B; pyramids and cones have one base, so theirs end in plus B. The 1/3 shows up on pyramids and cones because they hold exactly one third of the matching prism or cylinder. And the only formulas that use s, the slant height, are the surface areas of pyramids and cones.
ask: Which letter is an area, B or p? (expected answer: B, the area of the base)
Which two formulas use the slant height s? (expected answer: surface area of a pyramid and surface area of a cone)
A cylinder is a prism with a circle base. What is B for a cylinder? (expected answer: πr<sup>2</sup>)
notes.watch: Students read the s in SA = ½ps + B as "side." It means slant height. The side of the base is used to find p. Have the student write "s = slant" next to both formulas on their copy of the sheet.

slides.title: Box: Volume and Surface Area
slides.board:
A shipping box is 12 in long, 8 in wide, and 5 in tall.

Find its volume and its surface area.

V = Bh    SA = ph + 2B

figure.alt: A box (rectangular prism). The front bottom edge (length) is labeled 12 in, the edge going back (width) is labeled 8 in, and the front vertical edge (height) is labeled 5 in.

steps: Perimeter of the base: p = 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 in

notes.say: Notice how I find B and p first, on their own lines, before I touch either formula. ph is the four side walls laid end to end: a long strip 40 inches around and 5 inches tall. Then 2B adds the top and the bottom. The face-by-face check gives the same answer, which shows you what the formula is really doing.
ask: What is the base area, and what is its unit? (expected answer: 96 square inches)
Why is the volume in cubic inches but the surface area in square inches? (expected answer: volume counts cubes inside; surface area adds flat areas)
notes.watch: The most common slip is using B where p belongs: 96 × 5 + 192 = 672. Ask: "Is p an area or a length?"

slides.title: Prisms and Cylinders: V = Bh
slides.board:
Any solid with two matching bases and straight sides: V = Bh.

Base shapeBVolume
RectanglelwV = lwh
Triangle½bhV = (½bh) × length
Circle (cylinder)πr2V = πr2h

Cylinder surface area: 2πrh (the label) + 2πr2 (two lids).

Diameter given? Halve it first.

figure.alt: A cylinder standing upright. A dashed radius from the center of the top circle to its edge is labeled r. A measurement line beside the cylinder, from top to bottom, is labeled h.

notes.say: Every prism works the same way: find the area of the base, then multiply by how far it stretches. A triangular prism, like a tent or a wedge of cheese, uses the triangle area from last week as B. A cylinder is a prism with a circle for a base, so πr<sup>2</sup>h is just B times h. For cylinder surface area, picture peeling the label off a can: it unrolls into a rectangle as wide as the circumference, 2πr, and as tall as the can. The two lids add 2πr<sup>2</sup>.
ask: A triangular prism has a triangle base with base 6 and height 4. What is B? (expected answer: 12)
A can has a diameter of 10 cm. What number goes in for r? (expected answer: 5)
notes.watch: Two errors dominate cylinders: using the diameter as the radius (the volume comes out four times too big) and doubling the radius instead of squaring it (3.14 × 5 × 2 instead of 3.14 × 5 × 5). Insist on a separate line that says "r = ___."

slides.title: Can: Volume and Surface Area
slides.board:
A can has a diameter of 8 cm and a height of 12 cm. Use 3.14 for π.

Find its volume and its surface area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 310 230' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 80 50 L 80 200 A 70 18 0 0 0 220 200 L 220 50' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='150' cy='50' rx='70' ry='18' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 80 200 A 70 18 0 0 1 220 200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='245' y1='50' x2='245' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='239' y1='50' x2='251' y2='50' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='239' y1='200' x2='251' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='255' y='130' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>12 cm</text><line x1='80' y1='50' x2='220' y2='50' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='150' y='44' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>8 cm</text></svg>
figure.alt: A cylinder standing upright. A dashed diameter across the top circle is labeled 8 cm. A measurement line beside the cylinder, from top to bottom, is labeled 12 cm.

notes.say: I always write the radius on its own line before anything else, because the GED loves to give the diameter. Then I compute the volume. For surface area I find the two parts separately, the label and the lids, and add them. Writing the parts separately makes it easy to spot if you forgot a lid.
ask: What would the volume be if you used 8 as the radius? (expected answer: 3.14 × 64 × 12 = 2,411.52, four times too big)
notes.watch: If the student answers 301.44 for the surface area, they found only the label. If they get 351.68, they added only one lid (301.44 + 50.24).

slides.title: Prisms and Cylinders Together
slides.board:
Name the formula and the numbers before computing. Use 3.14 for π.

  1. A cube has 4-ft edges. Find V and SA.
  2. A tent is a triangular prism: the triangle has base 6 ft and height 4 ft, and the tent is 10 ft long. Find V.
  3. A tank is a cylinder with diameter 10 ft and height 6 ft. Find V.
  4. One cubic foot holds about 7.5 gallons. About how many gallons does the tank in #3 hold?

figure.alt: Wedo problem 2: a tent shaped like a triangular prism. The front triangle has a base labeled 6 ft and a dashed height labeled 4 ft. The length of the tent is labeled 10 ft.

steps: 1. B = 4 × 4 = 16; V = 16 × 4 = 64 ft3. Six faces of 16: SA = 96 ft2.

notes.say: Let's do these together. Before any arithmetic, tell me two things: which formula, and what number goes in each letter. I will reveal each line after you tell me your plan. Number 4 is a real-world extra step the GED likes: convert cubic feet into gallons.
ask: In number 2, what is B, and what plays the role of h? (expected answer: B = 12, the triangle area; h is the 10-ft length of the tent)
In number 3, what is r? (expected answer: 5)
notes.answer: (1) V = 64 ft<sup>3</sup>, SA = 96 ft<sup>2</sup>   (2) 120 ft<sup>3</sup>   (3) 471 ft<sup>3</sup>   (4) 3,532.5 gallons
notes.watch: On number 2, 240 means the ½ in the triangle area was dropped. On number 3, 1,884 means the diameter was used as the radius. On number 4, 62.8 means the student divided by 7.5 instead of multiplying: more cubic feet should mean more gallons.

slides.title: Your Turn: Prisms and Cylinders
slides.board:
Three minutes. Use 3.14 for π.

  1. Volume of a box 9 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm
  2. Surface area of the same box
  3. Volume of a cylinder with radius 3 in and height 7 in
  4. Surface area of a cylinder with diameter 2 m and height 5 m

notes.say: Your turn. I am starting the clock for three minutes. Write the formula, then the formula with your numbers, then the answer with units. When time is up, read me your four answers.
ask: Read me your four answers with units. (expected answer: 180 cm<sup>3</sup>, 202 cm<sup>2</sup>, 197.82 in<sup>3</sup>, 37.68 m<sup>2</sup>)
notes.answer: (1) B = 9 × 5 = 45; V = 45 × 4 = 180 cm<sup>3</sup>   (2) p = 28; ph = 28 × 4 = 112; 2B = 90; SA = 202 cm<sup>2</sup>   (3) 3.14 × 9 × 7 = 197.82 in<sup>3</sup>   (4) r = 1; 2πrh = 2 × 3.14 × 1 × 5 = 31.4; 2πr<sup>2</sup> = 6.28; SA = 37.68 m<sup>2</sup>
notes.watch: On number 2, 157 means one base was counted instead of two (112 + 45). On number 4, 87.92 means the diameter 2 was used as r (62.8 + 25.12), and 34.54 means only one lid was added (31.4 + 3.14).

slides.title: Pyramids and Cones: 1/3, h, and s
slides.board:
A pyramid or cone holds 1/3 of the prism or cylinder with the same base and height.

  • Pyramid: V = (1/3)Bh   SA = ½ps + B
  • Cone: V = (1/3)πr2h   SA = πrs + πr2

h = straight up the middle (volume). s = down the outside (surface area only).

h, r (or half the base edge), and s form a right triangle: s2 = h2 + r2. s is always the longest.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 0 240 200' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='150,30 60,200 240,200' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='none'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='60' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='240' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 0 240 200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 1 240 200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='150' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150' y1='200' x2='240' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='150,190 160,190 160,200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='144' y='125' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>h</text><text x='195' y='218' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>r</text><text x='205' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>s</text></svg>
figure.alt: A cone standing on its circular base. A dashed line from the tip straight down to the center of the base, at a right angle to the base, is labeled h (the height). A dashed radius from the center to the edge of the base is labeled r. The slanted side from the tip to the edge of the base is labeled s (the slant height).

notes.say: Picture filling a cone-shaped cup with water and pouring it into a can with the same base and height: it takes three cupfuls to fill the can. That is the 1/3. Now the most important distinction of the day: the height runs straight up the middle, at a right angle to the base, and the slant height runs down the outside face. Volume always uses the height. Only the pyramid and cone surface areas use the slant height. And because h, the radius, and s make a right triangle, last week's Pythagorean theorem finds whichever one is missing.
ask: A cone shows a height of 8 and a slant height of 10. Which goes into the volume formula? (expected answer: 8, the height)
Which is longer, the height or the slant height? Why? (expected answer: the slant height, because it is the hypotenuse of the right triangle)
notes.watch: If a figure shows both measurements, students grab the bigger number or the one drawn on the outside. Have them trace h with a finger (straight down the middle to the center of the base) and say "volume uses h" aloud.

slides.title: Square Pyramid
slides.board:
A square pyramid has base edges of 8 ft, a height of 3 ft, and a slant height of 5 ft.

Find its volume and its surface area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='40,220 240,220 290,175 165,30' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='240' y2='220' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='40' y1='220' x2='90' y2='175' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='90' y1='175' x2='290' y2='175' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='90' y2='175' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='165' y2='197' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='165,187 175,187 175,197' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='140' y2='220' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='2,3'/><text x='171' y='150' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>3 ft</text><text x='143' y='150' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>5 ft</text><text x='120' y='244' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>8 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A square pyramid. The front edge of the square base is labeled 8 ft. A dashed line from the top straight down to the center of the base, at a right angle, is labeled 3 ft (the height). A dotted line from the top down the middle of the front face to the middle of the front base edge is labeled 5 ft (the slant height).

steps: Base: B = 8 × 8 = 64 ft<sup>2</sup>; perimeter p = 4 × 8 = 32 ft
Surface area uses s: SA = ½ps + B = ½ × 32 × 5 + 64 = 80 + 64 = 144 ft2
Check the faces: each triangle is ½ × 8 × 5 = 20; four of them = 80; plus the base 64 = 144 ✓
Check s: half the base edge is 4, and 3<sup>2</sup> + 4<sup>2</sup> = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5<sup>2</sup> ✓

notes.say: Two letters, two jobs. For volume I use the height, 3. For surface area I use the slant height, 5, because the slant height is the height of each triangular face. Notice the right triangle inside: half of the base edge, the height, and the slant height. That is how the GED can give you two of them and expect you to find the third.
ask: Why does the volume use 3 and not 5? (expected answer: volume uses the height, the straight-up distance)
What is the area of one triangular face? (expected answer: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 ft<sup>2</sup>)
notes.watch: A volume of 192 means the 1/3 was forgotten; 106.67 (about) means the slant height was used for volume. A surface area of 80 means the base was left off.

slides.title: Cone: Find s, Then Surface Area
slides.board:
A cone has a radius of 5 in and a height of 12 in. Use 3.14 for π.

Find its slant height, its surface area, and its volume.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 0 240 200' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='150,30 60,200 240,200' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='none'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='60' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='240' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 0 240 200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 1 240 200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='150' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150' y1='200' x2='240' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='150,190 160,190 160,200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='144' y='125' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>12 in</text><text x='195' y='218' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>5 in</text><text x='205' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>s = ?</text></svg>
figure.alt: A cone standing on its circular base. A dashed line from the tip straight down to the center of the base, at a right angle to the base, is labeled 12 in (the height). A dashed radius from the center to the edge of the base is labeled 5 in. The slanted side from the tip to the edge of the base is labeled s = ? (the slant height).

steps: Right triangle: s2 = 122 + 52 = 144 + 25 = 169, so s = 13 in

notes.say: Here the slant height is missing, so we find it first with the Pythagorean theorem: the radius and the height are the legs, and the slant height is the hypotenuse. Then each formula gets its own measurement. A calculator trick for the 1/3: divide the height by 3 first when it divides evenly, and the numbers stay small.
ask: Which side of the right triangle is the slant height? (expected answer: the hypotenuse, the longest side)
In the surface area, what does πr<sup>2</sup> stand for? (expected answer: the circular base)
notes.watch: Students sometimes add 12 + 5 = 17 for the slant height. Remind them: the Pythagorean theorem adds the squares, then takes the square root.

slides.title: Pyramids and Cones Together
slides.board:
Use 3.14 for π. Say which measurement you will use before computing.

  1. Volume of a cone: radius 3 cm, height 10 cm
  2. Volume of a pyramid with a rectangular base 6 ft by 4 ft and height 9 ft
  3. Surface area of a square pyramid: base edge 12 in, slant height 10 in
  4. A cone has diameter 16 cm and slant height 17 cm. Find its height.

notes.say: Together now. For each one, tell me: is this volume or surface area, and so do I need h or s? Number 4 runs the Pythagorean theorem backward: we know the hypotenuse, so we subtract the squares.
ask: In number 3, what is p, and what is B? (expected answer: p = 4 × 12 = 48 in; B = 12 × 12 = 144 in<sup>2</sup>)
In number 4, why do we subtract 64 from 289? (expected answer: 17 is the hypotenuse, so leg<sup>2</sup> = hypotenuse<sup>2</sup> − other leg<sup>2</sup>)
notes.watch: On number 1, 282.6 means no 1/3. On number 2, 216 means no 1/3. On number 4, about 18.79 means the squares were added instead of subtracted, and about 5.74 means the diameter 16 was used instead of the radius 8; walk through which side is the hypotenuse.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Cone Volume
slides.board:
A pile of sand is shaped like a cone with a radius of 9 ft, a height of 12 ft, and a slant height of 15 ft. Use 3.14 for π.

About how many cubic feet of sand are in the pile?

A. 1,017.36    B. 1,271.70    C. 3,052.08    D. 4,069.44

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 0 240 200' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='150,30 60,200 240,200' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='none'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='60' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='240' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 0 240 200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 60 200 A 90 22 0 0 1 240 200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150' y1='30' x2='150' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150' y1='200' x2='240' y2='200' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='150,190 160,190 160,200' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='144' y='125' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>12 ft</text><text x='195' y='218' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>9 ft</text><text x='205' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>15 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A cone standing on its circular base. A dashed line from the tip straight down to the center of the base, at a right angle to the base, is labeled 12 ft (the height). A dashed radius from the center to the edge of the base is labeled 9 ft. The slanted side from the tip to the edge of the base is labeled 15 ft (the slant height).

steps: Eliminate D (4,069.44): it uses 18, the diameter, as the radius: (1/3) × 3.14 × 324 × 12. The radius is given as 9.
Eliminate C (3,052.08): it forgets the 1/3: 3.14 × 81 × 12. A cone holds one third of the matching cylinder.
Eliminate B (1,271.70): it uses the slant height 15 instead of the height: (1/3) × 3.14 × 81 × 15. Volume uses the straight-up height.

notes.say: Here is a real GED-style item. Notice the question gives you three measurements, and only two belong in the volume formula. Every wrong choice is built from a specific mistake: the diameter, the missing 1/3, or the slant height. Work it on paper first, then use the other choices as a checklist of traps you avoided.
ask: Which choice did you get, and which measurement did you leave out? (expected answer: A, 1,017.36; the slant height 15 is not used)
notes.watch: If the student chose B, C, or D, read the matching elimination aloud and have them find the exact line in their own work where they made that move.

slides.title: Spheres and Hemispheres
slides.board:
A sphere needs only the radius.

  • V = (4/3)πr3   (r3 = r × r × r)
  • SA = 4πr2
  • Hemisphere (half a sphere): V = ½ × (4/3)πr3 = (2/3)πr3

"In terms of π": leave π as a symbol. r = 3: V = (4/3)π(27) = 36π

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 230' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='115' r='85' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 65 115 A 85 20 0 0 0 235 115' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><path d='M 65 115 A 85 20 0 0 1 235 115' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><circle cx='150' cy='115' r='2' fill='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='150' y1='115' x2='235' y2='115' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='192' y='108' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>r</text></svg>
figure.alt: A sphere with a dashed circle around its middle. A line from the center of the sphere to its surface (the radius) is labeled r.

notes.say: Balls, globes, and round tanks are spheres. There is only one measurement, the radius, so the only traps are the diameter and the exponent. r cubed means the radius times itself three times, not 3 times the radius. A dome is usually half a sphere, a hemisphere, so you take half of the sphere's volume. And when a question says "in terms of π," you do all the arithmetic except the π, and leave π in the answer like a unit.
ask: What is 4<sup>3</sup>? (expected answer: 64, not 12)
A ball has a 20-inch diameter. What is r? (expected answer: 10 in)
notes.watch: On the calculator, students often enter 4/3 × 3.14 × 5 × 3 for r<sup>3</sup>. Show them the ^ key, or have them write 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 on paper first.

slides.title: Ball: Volume and Surface Area
slides.board:
A ball has a diameter of 12 inches. Use 3.14 for π.

Find its volume and surface area, in terms of π and as decimals.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 230' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='115' r='85' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 65 115 A 85 20 0 0 0 235 115' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><path d='M 65 115 A 85 20 0 0 1 235 115' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><circle cx='150' cy='115' r='2' fill='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='65' y1='115' x2='235' y2='115' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150' y='108' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>12 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: A sphere with a dashed circle around its middle. A line straight across the sphere through its center (the diameter) is labeled 12 in.

notes.say: First the radius, then the cube. Dividing 216 by 3 before multiplying by 4 keeps the numbers friendly. Writing 288π first gives you the "in terms of π" answer for free, and one more multiplication gives the decimal.
ask: What would the volume be if you used 12 as the radius? (expected answer: (4/3)π × 1,728 = 2,304π, eight times too big)
notes.watch: A volume of 75.36 means r<sup>3</sup> was computed as 3 × 6 = 18. A volume of 7,234.56 means the diameter 12 was used as r. A volume of 2,712.96 means the ÷ 3 was skipped. Have the student write r = 6 and r<sup>3</sup> = 216 on their own lines first.

slides.title: Composite Solids and Working Backward
slides.board:
Composite solid: split it into solids you know.

  • Pieces stacked together: add their volumes.
  • A hole or a hollow: subtract.

Working backward: volume given, a length missing.

  1. Write the formula.
  2. Substitute every number you know.
  3. Simplify, then divide to solve.

Cylinder: 471 = 3.14 × 25 × h → 471 = 78.5h → h = 6

notes.say: Real objects are rarely one perfect solid. A silo is a cylinder with a dome, a pipe is a cylinder with a cylinder removed, an ice cream cone is a cone with a half ball on top. Split the object into pieces, find each piece with its own formula, then add or subtract. Some GED questions run the formula in reverse: they give you the volume and ask for the height or the depth. Write the formula, put in what you know, multiply out everything you can, and divide.
ask: A grain silo is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top. Add or subtract? (expected answer: add)
A cylinder holds 100π cubic feet and has radius 5. What is its height? (expected answer: 25πh = 100π, so h = 4 ft)
notes.watch: In composite problems, watch for parts that share a radius but not a height. Have the student label each piece separately with its own r and h.

slides.title: Grain Bin: Cylinder Plus Cone
slides.board:
A grain bin is a cylinder with radius 5 ft and height 12 ft, topped by a cone-shaped roof with the same radius and a height of 3 ft. Use 3.14 for π.

What is the total volume?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 310 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='90' y='90' width='120' height='150' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='90,90 210,90 150,40' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='90' x2='210' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='180' y='108' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>5 ft</text><line x1='70' y1='90' x2='70' y2='240' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='64' y1='90' x2='76' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='64' y1='240' x2='76' y2='240' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='62' y='170' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>12 ft</text><line x1='230' y1='40' x2='230' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='224' y1='40' x2='236' y2='40' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='224' y1='90' x2='236' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='240' y='70' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>3 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: Side view of a cylinder with a cone on top. A dashed radius across the top of the cylinder is labeled 5 ft. A measurement line beside the cylinder is labeled 12 ft. A measurement line beside the cone, from its base to its tip, is labeled 3 ft.

steps: The pieces are stacked, so add: 942 + 78.5 = 1,020.5 ft3
Sense check: the roof is short and holds one third of a short cylinder, so it should add only a little. ✓

notes.say: Two pieces, two formulas, one addition. Notice the cone uses its own height, 3 feet, not the 12 feet of the cylinder. A quick sense check catches big mistakes: a short roof cannot hold more than the main bin.
ask: What height goes into the cone formula? (expected answer: 3 ft, the height of the roof only)
notes.watch: A total of 1,177.5 means the cone was computed without the 1/3 (942 + 235.5). A total near 1,256 means the 12-ft height was used for the cone as well.

slides.title: Composite and Backward Together
slides.board:
Use 3.14 for π.

  1. A rectangular tank has a base 4 ft by 3 ft and holds 60 ft3. How tall is it?
  2. A cylinder holds 628 cm3 and has radius 5 cm. Find its height.
  3. A wooden cube with 10-in edges has a cylinder-shaped hole (radius 2 in) drilled straight through it. What volume of wood is left?
  4. An ice cream cone (radius 2 in, height 6 in) is filled and topped with a hemisphere of radius 2 in. Total volume to the nearest hundredth?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='90,90 210,90 150,240' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 90 90 A 60 60 0 0 1 210 90' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='90' x2='210' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='180' y='108' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>2 in</text><line x1='230' y1='90' x2='230' y2='240' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='224' y1='90' x2='236' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='224' y1='240' x2='236' y2='240' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='240' y='170' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>6 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: Wedo problem 4: side view of an ice cream cone, a cone pointing down with a hemisphere on top. A dashed radius across the top is labeled 2 in. A measurement line from the top of the cone to its tip is labeled 6 in.

notes.say: These mix the two new ideas. For 1 and 2, tell me what you know and what you are solving for, then we divide. For 3, decide whether we add or subtract. For 4, remember a hemisphere is half a sphere.
ask: In number 3, do we add or subtract the cylinder? Why? (expected answer: subtract, because the hole is wood that was removed)
In number 4, what is r<sup>3</sup>? (expected answer: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8)
notes.watch: On number 2, 200 means the student divided 628 by 3.14 and stopped (forgot the r<sup>2</sup>). On number 4, about 58.61 means a whole sphere was added instead of half.

slides.title: Your Turn: Cones, Spheres, and More
slides.board:
Three minutes. Use 3.14 for π unless told otherwise.

  1. Surface area of a sphere with radius 5 cm
  2. Volume of a sphere with diameter 6 ft, in terms of π
  3. Volume of a cone with radius 4 m and height 6 m
  4. A cylinder with radius 2 in holds 50.24 in3. How tall is it?

notes.say: On your own now. Three minutes on the clock. Watch every radius, every exponent, and every 1/3. Then read me your answers.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 314 cm<sup>2</sup>, 36π ft<sup>3</sup>, 100.48 m<sup>3</sup>, 4 in)
notes.watch: On number 2, 288π means the diameter was used as r. On number 3, 301.44 means the 1/3 was dropped. On number 4, 8 means the student used 3.14 × 2 = 6.28 (doubling instead of squaring the radius).

slides.title: Scale Drawings and Scale Factors
slides.board:
Scale 1 in : 6 ft means each inch on the drawing is 6 real feet.

Real length = drawing length × 6. Convert lengths first, then find area or volume.

Scale factor kLengthsAreaVolume
2× 2× 4× 8
3× 3× 9× 27
½× ½× ¼× ⅛
k× k× k2× k3

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 215' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='30,130 50.0,110.0 100.0,110.0 80,130' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='80,130 100.0,110.0 100.0,160.0 80,180' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='30' y='130' width='50' height='50' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='55.0' y='198' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>1 unit</text><polygon points='150,70 194.0,26.0 304.0,26.0 260,70' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='260,70 304.0,26.0 304.0,136.0 260,180' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='150' y='70' width='110' height='110' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='205.0' y='198' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>2 units</text></svg>
figure.alt: Two cubes: a small cube with edges labeled 1 unit and a large cube with edges labeled 2 units. The large cube is twice as long, wide, and tall, so it holds 8 of the small cubes.

notes.say: Maps, blueprints, and models shrink or enlarge every length by the same number. For lengths, just multiply by the scale. The trap is area and volume. If every length doubles, a rectangle gets twice as long and twice as wide, so its area is four times as big. A box gets twice as long, wide, and tall, so it holds eight times as much. The safest method: change every length to real size first, then use the formula.
ask: A photo is enlarged so every length triples. How many times as much paper does the print need? (expected answer: 9)
Every edge of a box is doubled. How many times as much does it hold? (expected answer: 8)
notes.watch: The classic error is scaling area by k instead of k<sup>2</sup>. Draw a 1-by-1 square and a 2-by-2 square and have the student count the four small squares.

slides.title: Floor Plan and Flooring Cost
slides.board:
A floor plan uses the scale 1 in : 8 ft. A room measures 2.5 in by 1.75 in on the plan. Flooring costs $3.50 per square foot.

Find the room's real area and the cost of flooring.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 330 205' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='50' y='40' width='200' height='130' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>Room</text><text x='150' y='192' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>2.5 in</text><text x='260' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>1.75 in</text><text x='150' y='25' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>Scale: 1 in : 8 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A floor plan drawing of a rectangle labeled Room. The long side is labeled 2.5 in and the short side is labeled 1.75 in. The plan says "Scale: 1 in : 8 ft."

steps: Check with k<sup>2</sup>: plan area 2.5 × 1.75 = 4.375 in<sup>2</sup>; 4.375 × 8<sup>2</sup> = 4.375 × 64 = 280 ✓

notes.say: I convert each length to real feet before I do anything else. Then the area and the cost are ordinary arithmetic. The check shows why: the area grew by 8 squared, which is 64, not by 8.
ask: What would the area be if you multiplied the plan area by 8 instead of 64? (expected answer: 35 ft<sup>2</sup>, far too small for a 20-by-14 room)
notes.watch: If the student multiplies the perimeter by the price, ask: "Is flooring sold by the foot around the room or by the square foot covering it?"

slides.title: Scale Factor and Volume
slides.board:
A can has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. A larger can has every dimension doubled.

How do the volumes compare? Answer in terms of π.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 35 150 L 35 210 A 25 6 0 0 0 85 210 L 85 150' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='60' cy='150' rx='25' ry='6' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='60' y1='150' x2='85' y2='150' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='72.5' y='142' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>3 cm</text><text x='91' y='180.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>10 cm</text><path d='M 150 40 L 150 210 A 50 12 0 0 0 250 210 L 250 40' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='200' cy='40' rx='50' ry='12' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='200' y1='40' x2='250' y2='40' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='225.0' y='32' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>6 cm</text><text x='256' y='125.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>20 cm</text></svg>
figure.alt: Two cylinders (cans). The small can has a radius labeled 3 cm and a height labeled 10 cm. The large can has a radius labeled 6 cm and a height labeled 20 cm.

steps: Large can: r = 6, h = 20. V = π × 6<sup>2</sup> × 20 = 720π cm<sup>3</sup>
Rule: k = 2, so volume × 23 = 8. The large can holds 8 times as much.

notes.say: Many students guess the bigger can holds twice as much. It holds eight times as much, because the radius doubles, which quadruples the circle base, and the height doubles too: 4 times 2 is 8. Computing both volumes is the safe way; the k cubed rule is the fast way, and they agree.
ask: If the dimensions were tripled, how many times as much would it hold? (expected answer: 27)
notes.watch: A student who says "4 times" has scaled the base area and forgotten the height. Ask: "Did the can get taller too?"

slides.title: Scale Together
slides.board:
1. Map scale 1 cm : 40 km. Two cities are 5.5 cm apart. Real distance?
  2. Blueprint scale 1 in : 12 ft. A real wall is 42 ft long. How long is it on the blueprint?
  3. A model boat is built at 1 : 50 and is 30 cm long. How long is the real boat, in meters?
  4. A 20 in2 photo is enlarged by a scale factor of 3. Area of the enlargement?

notes.say: Together again. For each one, decide: am I going from drawing to real life (multiply) or from real life to drawing (divide)? And is the answer a length, an area, or a volume?
ask: In number 2, why do we divide? (expected answer: we are going from real size to drawing size, which is smaller)
In number 3, how many centimeters are in a meter? (expected answer: 100)
notes.watch: On number 4, 60 means the student multiplied the area by 3 instead of 9. On number 3, 1,500 m means the centimeters were never converted.

slides.title: Your Turn: Scale
slides.board:
Three minutes.

  1. Scale 1 in : 5 ft. A room is 3 in by 4.4 in on the plan. Real area?
  2. A cube with 3-cm edges is enlarged by a scale factor of 4. New volume?
  3. A model car is built at 1 : 24 and is 8 in long. How long is the real car, in feet?
  4. Every edge of a box is doubled. The small box has a surface area of 52 in2. Surface area of the large box?

notes.say: Last solo round. Three minutes. Convert lengths before areas and volumes, and watch your units. Then read me your four answers.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 330 ft<sup>2</sup>, 1,728 cm<sup>3</sup>, 16 ft, 208 in<sup>2</sup>)
notes.answer: (1) 15 ft × 22 ft = 330 ft<sup>2</sup>   (2) new edge 12; 12<sup>3</sup> = 1,728 cm<sup>3</sup> (or 27 × 64)   (3) 8 × 24 = 192 in = 16 ft   (4) surface area is an area: 52 × 2<sup>2</sup> = 208 in<sup>2</sup>
notes.watch: On number 2, 108 means the volume was multiplied by 4 instead of 64. On number 4, 416 means the student used the volume rule (× 8) for a surface area.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Scale Factor and Volume
slides.board:
An oatmeal container is a cylinder that holds 80 cubic inches. A family-size container has a radius and a height that are each 1.5 times those of the original.

How many cubic inches does the family-size container hold?

A. 120    B. 180    C. 270    D. 360
steps: Eliminate A (120): it multiplies the volume by 1.5 only. Volume grows by the cube of the scale factor.
Eliminate B (180): it multiplies by 1.52 = 2.25. That is the rule for area, and it ignores the taller height.
Eliminate D (360): it multiplies by 1.5 × 3 = 4.5. Cubing means 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5, not 1.5 × 3.

notes.say: This is the scale-factor trap in GED form. You do not need the radius or the height at all, only the rule: when every length is multiplied by k, the volume is multiplied by k cubed. If you are unsure, test it with numbers: make the original radius 1 and height 1 and compute both.
ask: What is 1.5<sup>3</sup>? (expected answer: 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 = 3.375)
notes.answer: C (270 in<sup>3</sup>). Volume scales by k<sup>3</sup> = 1.5<sup>3</sup> = 3.375; 80 × 3.375 = 270.
notes.watch: If the student chose B, ask whether the container got taller as well as wider. If D, have them type 1.5 ^ 3 into the calculator and compare with 1.5 × 3.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Let the Sheet Remember, You Choose
slides.board:
1. Fill or cover? Decide volume or surface area.
  2. Find the solid on the formula sheet.
  3. List the letters: r = __, h = __, s = __, B = __, p = __. Halve any diameter. h for volume, s for surface area.
  4. Read the π instruction: "use 3.14," "in terms of π," or "round to the nearest tenth."
  5. Check units: cubic for volume, square for area.

notes.say: The formula sheet removes memorizing, so GED geometry questions test choosing: the right formula and the right measurement. The wrong answer choices are built from the same mix-ups we practiced: diameter for radius, slant height for height, a missing 1/3, area instead of perimeter. Ten seconds listing your letters saves the point. On the calculator part, the TI-30XS has a π key and a ^ key for cubes. If the question says "use 3.14," use 3.14, because the π key can give a slightly different answer that may not match the choices.
ask: A problem gives a cone's diameter, height, and slant height, and asks for volume. Which two numbers do you use, and how? (expected answer: half the diameter for r, and the height)
notes.watch: Some students skip the letter list because it feels slow. Time it once: it takes about ten seconds and catches the errors that every distractor is built on.

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
• Volume fills (cubic units); surface area covers (square units).
  • B is the base area, p is the base perimeter. Prisms and cylinders: V = Bh.
  • Pyramids and cones hold 1/3. Volume uses h; their surface area uses s. s2 = h2 + r2.
  • Spheres: radius only; r3 = r × r × r. Composite: add or subtract pieces.
  • Scale: lengths × k, area × k2, volume × k3.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A → Exit Check

notes.say: That is the whole lesson in five lines. Tell me which line feels solid and which one you want more practice with. Next, work through the Student Lesson: it walks through each solid with a check on every screen. Then do Practice Set A. If you score under 80 percent, do Set B, which practices the same skills with different questions. Finish with the Exit Check; passing is 6 out of 8.
ask: Name one trap from today and how you will avoid it. (expected answer: any accurate one, for example "halve the diameter before using r" or "volume uses h, not s")

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
Last week you measured flat shapes. This week you measure solids: boxes, cans, cones, balls, and the scale drawings used to plan them. Work through one screen at a time. Most screens teach one idea, show a worked example, and end with a check you answer before moving on.

By the end, you will be able to:

  • Tell volume from surface area and read the GED formula sheet (B, p, h, s, r).
  • Find the volume and surface area of prisms and cylinders.
  • Find the volume and surface area of pyramids and cones, choosing height or slant height.
  • Work with spheres, composite solids, and missing dimensions.
  • Use scale drawings and scale factors for lengths, areas, and volumes.

Keep a calculator, paper, and a copy of the formula sheet (or this week's Study Sheet) next to you. Use 3.14 for π unless a problem says otherwise.

screens.title: Volume or Surface Area?
screens.html:
Every solid has two different measurements.

Volume is the space inside. It answers "How much does it hold?" Units are cubic: in3, ft3, m3. Think of counting unit cubes that fill the solid.

Surface area is the total area of every outside face. It answers "How much material covers it?" Units are square: in2, ft2.

Look for the action in the question. Fill, hold, pour, capacity point to volume. Paint, wrap, cover, label, line point to surface area. The object does not decide; the question does. The air inside a basketball is volume, but the leather on it is surface area.

example.prompt: A box is 3 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft tall. How many 1-foot cubes fit inside?
steps: One layer on the bottom holds 3 × 2 = 6 cubes.
The box is 2 layers tall, so 6 × 2 = 12 cubes.
example.answer: 12 cubes, so the volume is 12 ft<sup>3</sup>

check.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Finding how much sand fills a sandbox is a {{0}} question, and the answer is measured in {{1}}.

why: Surface area measures what covers the outside, like paint or a tarp. Sand fills the inside, so this is volume.
Perimeter is the distance around a flat shape. Sand fills a space, so you need volume.
Square feet measure a flat area, such as surface area. Volume counts cubes, so its units are cubic.
Feet measure a length, such as a perimeter. Volume is measured in cubic units.

check.hint: Is the sand filling the box or covering it?
check.explain:
Sand fills the sandbox, so this is a volume question, and volume is measured in cubic feet.

A common slip is to choose square feet. Square units are for flat areas like surface area.

screens.title: Reading the Formula Sheet
screens.html:
You do not need to memorize these formulas. The GED gives you a formula sheet. You need to know what each letter means.

LetterMeaning
BArea of the base (an area). Rectangle: lw. Triangle: ½bh. Circle: πr2.
pPerimeter of the base (a length). Add the sides of the base.
hHeight: straight up from the base, at a right angle.
sSlant height: down the outside of a pyramid or cone.
rRadius: half the diameter.

Three-line method: (1) write the formula; (2) rewrite it with your numbers; (3) compute and write units.

example.prompt: A prism has a rectangular base 7 cm by 3 cm and a height of 5 cm. Find B and p.
steps: p is a length around the base: 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 cm.

check.prompt: A square pyramid has base edges of 5 cm. In the formula SA = ½ps + B, what number replaces p?

mistakes.why: That is B, the area of the base (5 × 5). The letter p is the perimeter of the base: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20.
That is the length of one edge. The perimeter goes all the way around the square base: 4 × 5 = 20.
You added only two sides. A square base has four sides: 4 × 5 = 20.

check.hint: p is the distance all the way around the base.
check.explain:
p is the perimeter of the base. The base is a square with 5-cm sides.

p = 4 × 5 = 20 cm.

25 is a tempting answer, but 25 is the area of the base, which is B.

screens.title: Rectangular Prisms: Volume
screens.html:
A rectangular prism is a box shape. It has two matching rectangular bases, one on the bottom and one on top.

V = Bh, where B = length × width. So for a box, V = l × w × h.

Think of it in layers: B tells you how many unit cubes cover the bottom, and h tells you how many layers are stacked up.

All three measurements must be in the same unit. If one is in inches and another is in feet, convert first.

example.prompt: A storage bin is 3 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2.5 ft tall. Find its volume.

check.prompt: A moving box is 18 inches long, 12 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. What is its volume?

mistakes.why: That is only B, the area of the base (18 × 12). Multiply by the height too: 216 × 10 = 2,160.
You added the three dimensions. Volume multiplies them: 18 × 12 × 10 = 2,160.
That is the surface area (the cardboard). The question asks how much the box holds: 18 × 12 × 10 = 2,160.

check.hint: Find the area of the base, then multiply by the height.
check.explain:
B = 18 × 12 = 216 in2

V = Bh = 216 × 10 = 2,160 in3

If you got 216, you stopped at the base area and forgot the height.

screens.title: Rectangular Prisms: Surface Area
screens.html:
Surface area adds the areas of all six faces of a box. The formula sheet does it in two parts:

SA = ph + 2B

  • ph is the four side walls. Unroll them and they make one long rectangle, p long and h tall.
  • 2B is the top and the bottom.

You can always check by adding the faces in pairs: 2(lw) + 2(lh) + 2(wh).

p is a length (add the sides). B is an area (multiply). Do not use one in place of the other.

example.prompt: A box is 10 in long, 6 in wide, and 4 in tall. Find its surface area.

check.skill: Surface area of a rectangular prism
check.prompt: A gift box is 8 inches long, 5 inches wide, and 3 inches tall. How many square inches of wrapping paper cover it exactly, with no overlap?

mistakes.why: That is the volume (8 × 5 × 3). Wrapping paper covers the outside, so find the surface area.
You counted the top and bottom only once (78 + 40). A box has two bases: SA = ph + 2B = 78 + 80 = 158.
You added one of each pair of faces (40 + 24 + 15). Each face has a matching face on the other side, so double it: 158.

check.hint: Find p and B first. Then use SA = ph + 2B.
check.explain:
B = 8 × 5 = 40 in2 and p = 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 in.

ph = 26 × 3 = 78 in2 (the four sides)

2B = 2 × 40 = 80 in2 (top and bottom)

SA = 78 + 80 = 158 in2

Check: 2(40) + 2(24) + 2(15) = 80 + 48 + 30 = 158. If you got 118, you counted only one base.

screens.title: Other Prisms: Triangle Bases
screens.html:
V = Bh works for any prism, not just boxes. A prism has two matching bases joined by flat sides. The base can be a triangle, like a tent, a wedge of cheese, or a roof attic.

  1. Find B with the area formula for the base shape. For a triangle, B = ½ × base × height of the triangle.
  2. Multiply by the length of the prism (the distance between the two triangles). On the formula sheet, that length is h.

A triangular prism has two different "heights": the height of the triangle (used for B) and the length of the prism (used as h). Keep them on separate lines.

example.prompt: A tent is a triangular prism. The triangle has a base of 6 ft and a height of 4 ft. The tent is 8 ft long. Find its volume.

check.prompt: A wedge of cheese is a triangular prism. Each triangle face has a base of 5 cm and a height of 8 cm. The wedge is 3 cm thick. What is its volume?

mistakes.why: You forgot the ½ in the triangle area. B = ½ × 5 × 8 = 20, and 20 × 3 = 60.
You added the three numbers. Find the triangle area first, then multiply by the thickness.

check.hint: Find the area of the triangle first. Then multiply by the thickness.
check.explain:
B = ½ × 5 × 8 = 20 cm2

V = Bh = 20 × 3 = 60 cm3

If you got 120, you used 5 × 8 for the triangle and forgot the ½.

screens.title: Cylinders: Volume
screens.html:
A cylinder is a prism with a circle for each base, like a can or a round tank. Its base area is the area of a circle, B = πr2, so:

V = πr2h

Two traps:

  • The problem gives the diameter. Halve it to get r before you do anything else.
  • r2 means r × r, not r × 2.

example.prompt: A water tank is a cylinder with a radius of 2 m and a height of 5 m. Use 3.14 for π. How much water can it hold?

check.prompt: A can has a diameter of 10 cm and a height of 14 cm. What is its volume? Use 3.14 for π.

mistakes.why: You used the diameter, 10, as the radius. The radius is half the diameter: r = 5, so V = 3.14 × 25 × 14 = 1,099.
You multiplied by r instead of r<sup>2</sup>. Square the radius: 5<sup>2</sup> = 25, so V = 3.14 × 25 × 14 = 1,099.
You found 2πrh, the area of the label around the can. Volume is πr<sup>2</sup>h = 3.14 × 25 × 14 = 1,099.

check.hint: The formula needs the radius. What is half of the diameter?
check.explain:
r = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm

V = πr2h = 3.14 × 52 × 14 = 3.14 × 25 × 14 = 1,099 cm3

If you got 4,396, you used the diameter as the radius, which makes the answer four times too big.

screens.title: Cylinders: Surface Area
screens.html:
Picture peeling the label off a can. It unrolls into a rectangle. Its width is the distance around the can, 2πr, and its height is h. Then add the two circle lids.

SA = 2πrh + 2πr2

  • 2πrh: the curved side (the label)
  • 2πr2: the top and bottom circles

Compute the two parts on separate lines and then add. That way it is easy to see if you left out a lid. If the object has no lid (an open bucket or a cup), use only one circle.

example.prompt: A can has a diameter of 6 cm and a height of 10 cm. Use 3.14 for π. Find its surface area.

check.prompt: A closed cylinder has a radius of 2 ft and a height of 9 ft. What is its surface area? Use 3.14 for π.

mistakes.why: That is only the curved side (2 × 3.14 × 2 × 9). Add the two circle ends: 2 × 3.14 × 4 = 25.12.
You added only one circle. A closed cylinder has two ends: 113.04 + 2(12.56) = 138.16.

check.hint: Find the curved side (2πrh) and the two ends (2πr<sup>2</sup>) separately, then add.
check.explain:
Curved side: 2πrh = 2 × 3.14 × 2 × 9 = 113.04 ft2

Two ends: 2πr2 = 2 × 3.14 × 4 = 25.12 ft2

SA = 113.04 + 25.12 = 138.16 ft2

If you got 125.6, you included only one end.

screens.title: Pyramids: Volume and Surface Area
screens.html:
A pyramid has one flat base and triangle faces that meet at a point. It holds exactly one third of a prism with the same base and height.

V = (1/3)Bh     SA = ½ps + B

  • Volume uses h, the height straight up from the center of the base to the top.
  • Surface area uses s, the slant height down the middle of a triangle face. ½ps adds up all the triangle faces; + B adds the one base.

example.prompt: A square pyramid has base edges of 10 ft, a height of 12 ft, and a slant height of 13 ft. Find its volume and surface area.

A dotted line from the top down the middle of the front face to the middle of the front base edge is labeled 13 ft (the slant height).

check.prompt: A square pyramid has base edges of 6 in, a height of 4 in, and a slant height of 5 in. What is its volume?

mistakes.why: You forgot the 1/3. A pyramid holds one third of the matching prism: (1/3) × 36 × 4 = 48.
You used the slant height, 5. Volume uses the height, 4: (1/3) × 36 × 4 = 48.
That is the surface area (½ × 24 × 5 + 36). The question asks for volume: (1/3)Bh = 48.

check.hint: Volume uses the height, not the slant height. Do not forget the 1/3.
check.explain:
B = 6 × 6 = 36 in2

V = (1/3)Bh = (1/3) × 36 × 4 = 12 × 4 = 48 in3

The slant height, 5, is not used for volume. If you got 60, you used it.

screens.title: Cones: Height or Slant Height?
screens.html:
A cone is like a pyramid with a circle base. It holds one third of the cylinder with the same radius and height.

V = (1/3)πr2h     SA = πrs + πr2

Volume always uses the height h (straight up the middle). Only the surface-area formula uses the slant height s (down the outside). If a drawing shows both, use each in its own place. The slant height is always the longer one.

Tip: when h divides by 3, do (1/3) × h first to keep the numbers small.

A dashed radius from the center to the edge of the base is labeled r. The slanted side from the tip to the edge of the base is labeled s (the slant height).

example.prompt: A paper cup is a cone with a radius of 4 cm and a height of 9 cm. Use 3.14 for π. Find its volume.

check.prompt: A cone has a radius of 3 cm, a height of 4 cm, and a slant height of 5 cm. What is its volume? Use 3.14 for π.

mistakes.why: You forgot the 1/3. That is the volume of the matching cylinder. Divide by 3: 37.68.
You used the slant height, 5. Volume uses the height, 4: (1/3) × 3.14 × 9 × 4 = 37.68.
That is the surface area (πrs + πr<sup>2</sup>). The question asks for volume.

check.hint: Which measurement goes straight up the middle? Use that one, and remember the 1/3.
check.explain:
V = (1/3)πr2h = (1/3) × 3.14 × 32 × 4 = (1/3) × 3.14 × 9 × 4

(1/3) × 9 = 3, so V = 3.14 × 3 × 4 = 3.14 × 12 = 37.68 cm3

If you got 47.1, you used the slant height instead of the height.

screens.title: Finding a Missing Slant Height or Height
screens.html:
Inside every cone is a right triangle: the height h and the radius r are the legs, and the slant height s is the hypotenuse. A square pyramid has the same triangle, using half of a base edge instead of r.

s2 = h2 + r2 (Pythagorean theorem from Week 5)

  • Missing s: add the squares, then take the square root.
  • Missing h: subtract, h2 = s2 − r2, then take the square root.

example.prompt: A cone has a radius of 5 in and a height of 12 in. Find its slant height and its surface area. Use 3.14 for π.

A dashed radius from the center to the edge of the base is labeled 5 in. The slanted side from the tip to the edge of the base is labeled s = ? (the slant height).

check.prompt: A square pyramid has base edges of 16 m and a height of 6 m. What is its slant height?

mistakes.why: You used the whole base edge, 16, as a leg. The slant height reaches the middle of a base edge, so the leg is half of 16, which is 8: 6<sup>2</sup> + 8<sup>2</sup> = 100.
You added 6 + 8. The Pythagorean theorem adds the squares: 36 + 64 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10.
You found s<sup>2</sup>. Take the square root: s = 10.

check.hint: Draw the right triangle: the height, half of a base edge, and the slant height.
check.explain:
The right triangle has legs h = 6 and half the base edge, 16 ÷ 2 = 8.

s2 = 62 + 82 = 36 + 64 = 100

s = √100 = 10 m

If you got about 17.1, you used the whole edge, 16, instead of half of it.

screens.title: Spheres and Hemispheres
screens.html:
A sphere is a ball shape. Its only measurement is the radius.

V = (4/3)πr3     SA = 4πr2

  • r3 means r × r × r. For r = 4, r3 = 64, not 12.
  • Given a diameter? Halve it first.
  • A hemisphere is half a sphere, like a dome or a bowl. Its volume is half of (4/3)πr3.

Calculator tip: multiply 4 × 3.14 × r3, then divide by 3 at the end.

example.prompt: A ball has a diameter of 12 inches. Use 3.14 for π. Find its volume.

check.prompt: A dome is shaped like a hemisphere (half of a sphere) with a diameter of 12 m. What is the volume of the dome? Use 3.14 for π.

mistakes.why: That is the volume of the whole sphere. A hemisphere is half: 904.32 ÷ 2 = 452.16.
You used the diameter, 12, as the radius. Halve it first: r = 6 and r<sup>3</sup> = 216.
You squared the radius instead of cubing it (6<sup>2</sup> = 36). Volume uses r<sup>3</sup> = 216.

check.hint: Find r first. Then find the volume of the whole sphere and take half.
check.explain:
r = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m, and r3 = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216

Whole sphere: (4/3) × 3.14 × 216 = 904.32 m3

Hemisphere: 904.32 ÷ 2 = 452.16 m3

If you got 904.32, you forgot that a dome is only half of a sphere.

screens.title: Answers in Terms of π
screens.html:
Some GED questions say "give your answer in terms of π." That means: do all the arithmetic except the π, and leave π in the answer like a label.

  • A cylinder with r = 3 and h = 5: V = π × 9 × 5 = 45π.
  • A sphere with r = 3: V = (4/3)π × 27 = 36π.

An answer in terms of π is exact. To change it to a decimal, multiply by 3.14 (or use the π key): 45π ≈ 141.3. Answer choices written with π are a signal not to multiply by 3.14 at all.

example.prompt: Find the volume of a cylinder with diameter 8 and height 3, in terms of π.

check.prompt: A cone has a radius of 6 and a height of 5. What is its volume, in terms of π?
why: You forgot the 1/3. π × 36 × 5 = 180π is the volume of the matching cylinder; a cone holds a third of it.
You did not square the radius: (1/3)π × 6 × 5 = 10π. The formula uses r<sup>2</sup> = 36.
You used 12, the diameter, as the radius: (1/3)π × 144 × 5 = 240π. The radius is given as 6.
check.hint: Use V = (1/3)πr<sup>2</sup>h and keep π as a symbol.
check.explain:
V = (1/3)πr2h = (1/3)π × 36 × 5

(1/3) × 36 = 12, and 12 × 5 = 60, so V = 60π.

180π is the most tempting wrong choice: it is the cylinder, not the cone.

screens.title: Composite Solids
screens.html:
A composite solid is made of two or more simple solids. A silo is a cylinder with a dome. A pencil is a cylinder with a cone. A pipe is a cylinder with a smaller cylinder removed.

  1. Split the object into solids you know.
  2. Find each volume with its own formula and its own measurements.
  3. Add pieces that are stacked together. Subtract a hole or a hollow part.

Label each piece separately. Two pieces often share a radius but not a height.

example.prompt: A grain bin is a cylinder (radius 5 ft, height 12 ft) with a cone roof (radius 5 ft, height 3 ft). Use 3.14 for π. Find the total volume.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 310 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='90' y='90' width='120' height='150' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='90,90 210,90 150,40' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='90' x2='210' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='180' y='108' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>5 ft</text><line x1='70' y1='90' x2='70' y2='240' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='64' y1='90' x2='76' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='64' y1='240' x2='76' y2='240' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='62' y='170' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>12 ft</text><line x1='230' y1='40' x2='230' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='224' y1='40' x2='236' y2='40' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='224' y1='90' x2='236' y2='90' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='240' y='70' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>3 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: Side view of a cylinder with a cone on top. A dashed radius across the top of the cylinder is labeled 5 ft. A measurement line beside the cylinder is labeled 12 ft. A measurement line beside the cone, from its base to its tip, is labeled 3 ft.

check.prompt: A model rocket is a cylinder with a cone on top. Both have a radius of 3 cm. The cylinder is 10 cm tall, and the cone is 4 cm tall. What is the total volume? Use 3.14 for π.

mistakes.why: You found the cone without the 1/3 (113.04). The cone holds one third of that: 37.68. Total: 282.6 + 37.68 = 320.28.
That is only the cylinder. Add the cone on top: 282.6 + 37.68 = 320.28.
That is only the cone. Add the cylinder: 282.6 + 37.68 = 320.28.

check.hint: Find the cylinder and the cone separately. Each uses its own height.

screens.title: Working Backward to a Missing Dimension
screens.html:
Sometimes the GED gives you the volume and asks for a height, depth, or radius. Use the same formula, run in reverse.

  1. Write the formula.
  2. Substitute every number you know, including the volume.
  3. Multiply out the known numbers.
  4. Divide to find the missing value.

Check by putting your answer back into the formula.

example.prompt: A cylinder holds 471 in<sup>3</sup> and has a radius of 5 in. Use 3.14 for π. How tall is it?

figure.alt: A cylinder standing upright. A dashed radius from the center of the top circle to its edge is labeled 5 in. A measurement line beside the cylinder, from top to bottom, is labeled h = ?.

check.prompt: A rectangular aquarium has a base that is 30 inches long and 12 inches wide. It holds 5,400 cubic inches of water. How deep is the water?

mistakes.why: You divided by the length only (5,400 ÷ 30). Divide by the whole base area: 30 × 12 = 360.
You divided by the width only (5,400 ÷ 12). Divide by the base area: 5,400 ÷ 360 = 15.
You added 30 + 12. The base area is 30 × 12 = 360, and 5,400 ÷ 360 = 15.

check.hint: V = Bh. Find B, then divide the volume by B.

screens.title: Scale Drawings: Lengths
screens.html:
A scale drawing (a map, blueprint, or model) shows a real object with every length changed by the same amount. A scale like 1 in : 8 ft means 1 inch on the drawing stands for 8 feet in real life.

  • Drawing to real: multiply by the scale.
  • Real to drawing: divide by the scale.
  • A scale like 1 : 24 has no units: 1 inch on the model is 24 inches on the real object. Convert units at the end if asked.

You can also set up a proportion: 1/8 = drawing/real.

example.prompt: A model car is built at a scale of 1 : 24. The model is 7.5 inches long. How long is the real car, in feet?

check.prompt: On a map, 1 inch represents 20 miles. Two towns are 4.25 inches apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?

mistakes.why: You added 20 to the map distance. Each inch stands for 20 miles, so multiply: 4.25 × 20 = 85.
You used only the 4 whole inches. Include the quarter inch: 4.25 × 20 = 85.
You divided 20 by 4.25. Going from the map to real life, multiply: 4.25 × 20 = 85.

check.hint: Each inch on the map stands for 20 miles.

screens.title: Scale Drawings: Area
screens.html:
To find a real area from a scale drawing, change each length to real size first, then use the area formula.

Do not multiply the drawing's area by the scale. Area uses two lengths, so it grows by the scale squared. With a scale of 1 in : 4 ft, each square inch on the drawing is 4 × 4 = 16 square feet.

example.prompt: A floor plan uses the scale 1 inch : 4 feet. A bedroom is 3.5 in by 2.75 in on the plan. Find the real floor area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 330 205' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='50' y='40' width='200' height='130' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>Bedroom</text><text x='150' y='192' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>3.5 in</text><text x='260' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>2.75 in</text><text x='150' y='25' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>Scale: 1 in : 4 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A floor plan drawing of a rectangle labeled Bedroom. The long side is labeled 3.5 in and the short side is labeled 2.75 in. The plan says "Scale: 1 in : 4 ft."

check.prompt: On a garden plan, 1 cm represents 2 m. A rectangular vegetable bed is 4.5 cm by 3 cm on the plan. What is the real area of the bed?

mistakes.why: You found the plan area (13.5 cm<sup>2</sup>) and multiplied by 2. Area grows by 2<sup>2</sup> = 4. Easier: change lengths first: 9 m × 6 m = 54.
That is the area on the plan, in square centimeters. Change each length to meters first: 9 m by 6 m.
That is the perimeter of the real bed (9 + 6 + 9 + 6). Area multiplies length by width: 9 × 6 = 54.

check.hint: Change both lengths to real meters before you multiply.
check.explain:
Length: 4.5 × 2 = 9 m. Width: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

Area: 9 × 6 = 54 m2

Check: the plan area is 13.5 cm2, and 13.5 × 22 = 13.5 × 4 = 54.

screens.title: Scale Factors: Area and Volume
screens.html:
When every length of a figure is multiplied by a scale factor k, the new figure is similar to the old one.

MeasureMultiplied byk = 2k = 3
Length, perimeterk23
Area, surface areak249
Volumek3827

Why? Volume multiplies three lengths, and each one grew by k. If you are unsure, find the new dimensions and compute directly.

example.prompt: A cube has 2-inch edges. Every edge is doubled. How does the volume change?
example.answer: The volume is 8 times as large.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 215' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='30,130 50.0,110.0 100.0,110.0 80,130' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='80,130 100.0,110.0 100.0,160.0 80,180' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='30' y='130' width='50' height='50' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='55.0' y='198' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>2 in</text><polygon points='150,70 194.0,26.0 304.0,26.0 260,70' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='260,70 304.0,26.0 304.0,136.0 260,180' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='150' y='70' width='110' height='110' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='205.0' y='198' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>4 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: Two cubes side by side. The small cube has edges labeled 2 in. The large cube has edges labeled 4 in.

check.prompt: A box is 1 ft by 3 ft by 5 ft, so its volume is 15 ft3. Every dimension is multiplied by 3. What is the volume of the new box?
why: You multiplied the volume by 3. All three dimensions grew by 3, so the volume grows by 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.
You multiplied by 3<sup>2</sup> = 9, which is the rule for area. Volume uses three dimensions: 15 × 27 = 405.
You added 3 to each dimension (4 × 6 × 8 = 192). A scale factor multiplies: 3 × 9 × 15 = 405.
check.hint: Find the new length, width, and height, or multiply the volume by 3 × 3 × 3.
check.explain:
New dimensions: 1 × 3 = 3, 3 × 3 = 9, 5 × 3 = 15.

V = 3 × 9 × 15 = 405 ft3

Check: 15 × 33 = 15 × 27 = 405. The tempting 45 multiplies by 3 only once.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Volume fills (cubic units). Surface area covers (square units).
  • On the formula sheet: B = base area, p = base perimeter, h = height, s = slant height, r = radius (half the diameter).
  • Prisms and cylinders: V = Bh. Cylinder: V = πr2h and SA = 2πrh + 2πr2.
  • Pyramids and cones hold 1/3 of the matching prism or cylinder. Volume uses h; their surface area uses s.
  • s2 = h2 + r2 (for a square pyramid, use half the base edge for r).
  • Sphere: V = (4/3)πr3, SA = 4πr2. A hemisphere is half.
  • Composite solids: add stacked pieces, subtract holes. Missing dimension: substitute, then divide.
  • Scale: convert lengths first. Scale factor k: lengths × k, area × k2, volume × k3.

Next: Practice Set A. If you score under 80%, practice the same skills again with Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

items.prompt: Drag each task into the correct category. Does the task call for finding volume or surface area?
choices: Water needed to fill a swimming pool
Paint needed to cover the outside of a shed
Wrapping paper needed to cover a gift box
Soil needed to fill a planter
Leather needed to cover a basketball
Concrete poured into a cylinder-shaped post form
items.why: The most common slip is putting the leather on the basketball under volume because a ball is "full." The leather only covers the outside, so it is surface area. Ask of each task: is the material going inside (volume) or on the outside (surface area)?
items.hint: Ask: is the material going inside the object (filling it) or on the outside (covering it)?
items.explain:
Volume measures what fills the inside of a solid. Surface area measures what covers the outside.

  • Water filling a pool: volume
  • Paint covering a shed: surface area
  • Wrapping paper covering a box: surface area
  • Soil filling a planter: volume
  • Leather covering a basketball: surface area
  • Concrete filling a post form: volume

A common slip is to put the basketball under volume because a ball is “full.” But the leather only covers the outside, so it is surface area.

items.prompt:
The GED formula sheet gives the surface area of a pyramid as

SA = ½ps + B

What does the letter p stand for?
options: The slant height of the pyramid
why: The height h is not in this formula at all; it is used in the volume formula V = (1/3)Bh. The letter p is a length that goes around the base.
That is what B stands for. B is an area (multiply); p is a length around the base (add the sides).
The slant height is s, the letter p is multiplied by. p is the perimeter of the base.
items.hint: On the formula sheet, B is an area and p is a length. Which length goes all the way around the base?
items.explain:
On the formula sheet, p is the perimeter of the base: the distance around the base. For a square base with 6-inch sides, p = 4 × 6 = 24 inches.

The other letters in the formula: s is the slant height and B is the area of the base. The height h does not appear in this formula at all; it is used in the volume formula V = (1/3)Bh.

“The area of the base” is the most common wrong choice, but that is what B stands for.

items.prompt: A fish tank is shaped like a rectangular prism. It is 30 inches long, 12 inches wide, and 16 inches tall. What is the volume of the tank?
why: That is the surface area, the glass covering the outside: 2(30 × 12) + 2(30 × 16) + 2(12 × 16) = 2,064. Volume is the space inside.
That is only B, the area of the base (30 × 12). Multiply by the height too: 360 × 16 = 5,760.
You added the three dimensions (30 + 12 + 16). Volume multiplies them: 30 × 12 × 16 = 5,760.
items.hint: Use V = Bh. The base is the 30 by 12 rectangle.
items.explain:
Use V = Bh.

Area of the base: B = 30 × 12 = 360 in2

V = 360 × 16 = 5,760 cubic inches

2,064 is the surface area: 2(30 × 12) + 2(30 × 16) + 2(12 × 16) = 720 + 960 + 384 = 2,064. That measures the glass, not the space inside. 360 is only the base area (the height was left out). 58 comes from adding the three dimensions.

items.prompt: On a hiking map, 1 centimeter represents 2.5 kilometers. A trail is 6.4 centimeters long on the map. How long is the real trail?

mistakes.why: You added 6.4 + 2.5. Each centimeter stands for 2.5 km, so multiply: 6.4 × 2.5 = 16.
You divided 6.4 by 2.5. Going from the map to real life, multiply: 6.4 × 2.5 = 16.
You used only the 6 whole centimeters (6 × 2.5). Include the 0.4 cm: 6.4 × 2.5 = 16.

items.hint: Each centimeter on the map stands for 2.5 km. Multiply.
items.explain:
Each centimeter on the map is 2.5 km in real life, so multiply:

6.4 × 2.5 = 16 km

Proportion check: 1/2.5 = 6.4/x, so x = 6.4 × 2.5 = 16. Dividing (2.56) gives a trail shorter than the map distance in centimeters, which cannot be right.

items.prompt:
A rain barrel is shaped like a cylinder. It has a diameter of 4 feet and a height of 6 feet. What is the volume of the rain barrel?

Use 3.14 for π. Round your answer to the nearest tenth.

mistakes.why: You used the diameter, 4, as the radius. Halve it first: r = 2, so V = 3.14 × 4 × 6 = 75.36, about 75.4.
You multiplied by r instead of r<sup>2</sup> (3.14 × 2 × 6). Square the radius: 2<sup>2</sup> = 4, so V = 3.14 × 4 × 6 = 75.36.

items.hint: The formula needs the radius. What is half of the diameter?
items.explain:
Formula: V = πr2h

The radius is half the diameter: r = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 ft

V = 3.14 × 22 × 6 = 3.14 × 4 × 6 = 3.14 × 24 = 75.36

Rounded to the nearest tenth: 75.4 cubic feet

If you use the diameter, 4, as the radius, you get 3.14 × 16 × 6 = 301.44, which is four times too large.

items.prompt:
Choose the word or expression that correctly completes each statement about the formula sheet.

In the cone volume formula V = (1/3)πr2h, the letter h stands for the {{0}} of the cone.

In the pyramid surface-area formula SA = ½ps + B, the letter s stands for the {{1}}.

For a cylinder, the base is a circle, so the area of the base, B, is equal to {{2}}.

why: The slant height runs down the outside of the cone and appears only in the surface-area formula. Volume uses the straight-up height.
The diameter is not in this formula; the radius r is. The letter h is the height from the base to the tip.
It is easy to read s as "side," but the side length of the base is used to find p. The letter s is the slant height down the middle of a triangle face.
SA is the surface area, the whole left side of the formula. The letter s is one measurement inside it: the slant height.
2πr is the circumference, a length around the circle. B is an area, and the area of a circle is πr<sup>2</sup>.
πd is also the circumference (π times the diameter), a length. B is the area of the circle: πr<sup>2</sup>.
2πrh is the area of the curved side of the cylinder (the label), not the base. The base is a circle with area πr<sup>2</sup>.

items.hint: Volume formulas use the straight-up height. B always means an area, and the area of a circle is on the formula sheet.
items.explain:
First blank: Volume formulas use the height, the straight-up distance from the base to the tip. The slant height is used only for surface area.

Second blank: In SA = ½ps + B, s is the slant height, the distance from the tip down the middle of a side face to the edge of the base. It is easy to think s means “side,” but the side length of the base is used to find p.

Third blank: B is the area of the base. A cylinder's base is a circle, and the area of a circle is πr2. That is why the cylinder volume formula V = πr2h is the same as V = Bh. The expressions 2πr and πd are the circumference (a length), and 2πrh is the area of the curved side.

items.prompt:
A planter is shaped like a cone. Its radius is 6 cm, its height is 8 cm, and its slant height is 10 cm, as shown.

About how much soil can the planter hold?

A dashed radius from the center to the edge of the base is labeled 6 cm. The slanted side from the tip to the edge of the base is labeled 10 cm.

why: You used the slant height, 10, instead of the height: (1/3) × π × 36 × 10 = 120π ≈ 377. Volume uses the straight-up height, 8.
